concept: Leveraged trading uncertainty calibration and cascade-model validation
summary: Source-anchored research for Leveraged trading uncertainty calibration and cascade-model validation. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn calibrate a confidence radius by inverting a concentration bound. They recommend bootstrap or cross-validation in practice because the a priori bound can be conservative. This recommendation does not itself establish a dependence-aware coverage theorem. (low confidence)

Li’s Wasserstein-Kelly concentration result requires independently drawn observations and a light-tailed distribution. Its statistical guarantee must retain those assumptions when used to calibrate a radius. (low confidence)

An overly rigid background rate can misattribute exogenous variation to self-excitation and inflate the estimated branching ratio. Filimonov and Sornette demonstrate spurious apparent criticality from regime-switching Poisson data, while Omi, Hirata and Aihara show branching-ratio overestimation when background variation is modeled too smoothly in their financial-data analysis. (high confidence)

An INAR approximation that ignores excitation within bins can become biased when the bin width exceeds the excitation timescale. Fine-bin asymptotic consistency does not establish reliable coarse-bin estimation. (medium confidence)

Deutsch and Ross explicitly model missingness or timing noise through a distortion function and use ABC-Hawkes because the observed-data likelihood becomes intractable. Their framework covers gaps, reduced detection probabilities and noisy timestamps; applying it to a throttled feed requires specifying an appropriate distortion model. (low confidence)

Rizoiu and collaborators fit interval-censored counts through a Mean Behavior Poisson process whose intensity equals the expected Hawkes intensity and whose parameters correspond to Hawkes parameters. Its interval-censored Poisson likelihood belongs to that surrogate process; Hawkes itself lacks independent increments, so the method must not be described as the exact count likelihood of a Hawkes process. (low confidence)

For independent, identically distributed observations and the specified exponential-tail assumption, Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn calibrate a Wasserstein radius by inverting a concentration bound at a prescribed failure probability. Their resulting ambiguity ball is a confidence set for the true distribution and yields a finite-sample out-of-sample cost bound. The concentration theorem reproduced in the Wasserstein-Kelly paper likewise explicitly requires independent samples and a light-tail condition; applying this route to dependent financial returns requires a separately justified result. (medium confidence)

Duchi, Glynn and Namkoong provide an alternative based on smooth f-divergence balls. Their dependent-data theorem for an aperiodic, positive Harris recurrent Markov chain requires sufficiently fast beta-mixing, Lipschitz and loss moment bounds, and a unique optimizer. Its coverage limit depends on the ratio of marginal loss variance to long-run loss variance, with the latter including lagged covariances. Thus an IID chi-square calibration cannot simply be carried over unchanged to serially dependent observations. The result is asymptotic coverage for the optimal objective, not finite-sample Wasserstein-ball coverage. (low confidence)

In their October 2026 preprint, Jung and Lee construct common-signal and stable nonnegative Hawkes models with identical means and Bartlett spectra but different excitation mechanisms. This is second-order non-identification, so spectral fit alone cannot identify structural cross-excitation in that model comparison. (low confidence)

Omi and colleagues explicitly state that their background-rate smoother is unsuitable for online estimation because it uses observations around the target time. A live cascade diagnostic cannot treat this retrospective fit as a causal-time estimator. (low confidence)

Validation design recommendation, inferred from these studies: benchmark against non-exciting regime-switching simulations, repeat estimation across aggregation scales, model the actual event-loss or timing-noise mechanism, and compare plausible background-rate specifications. These checks address demonstrated estimator failure modes; they do not establish trading profitability. (medium confidence)

Shlomovich, Cohen and Adams estimate multivariate binned Hawkes parameters with Monte Carlo expectation–maximization over latent event times. In their simulation study this approach outperforms the compared alternatives in mean squared error; the paper does not establish universal superiority over all count estimators. (low confidence)

Blanchet, Kang and Murthy calibrate uncertainty using robust Wasserstein profile inference: find the minimum transport cost needed to make an estimating equation hold, then use a confidence-level quantile of that profile to make the population-optimal parameter plausible. This targets a confidence region for an optimal parameter rather than requiring coverage of the entire true distribution. Their general setup assumes IID observations, and their practical quantile approximation uses asymptotic analysis; Gao explicitly identifies the asymptotic limitation of this approach. (medium confidence)

Gao develops non-asymptotic, loss-sensitive Wasserstein DRO guarantees using concentration controlled by loss variation and localized Rademacher complexity. The analysis relates radius selection to Lipschitz or gradient variation instead of only full-distribution coverage. Its setup uses IID samples and distributional concentration assumptions, including transportation-information inequalities; it is not a general certificate for heavy-tailed, serially dependent Kelly returns. (low confidence)

A radius chosen to cover the entire data-generating distribution can be conservative in moderate or high dimension. Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn recommend bootstrap or cross-validation calibration in practice, while Gao distinguishes this distribution-coverage approach from guarantees adapted to the loss family. Practical tuning should therefore state which guarantee it targets, rather than equating good validation performance with distribution coverage. (medium confidence)

With interval-censored event counts, the ordinary event-time Hawkes log-likelihood cannot be evaluated directly because exact event times are unavailable; aggregation therefore requires an observation-aware estimator rather than treating bin timestamps as exact events. (high confidence)

Missing-event inference differs from ordinary count aggregation: unobserved Hawkes events still excite later events. Deutsch and Ross explicitly model detection or timestamp distortion and use approximate Bayesian computation; some distortion parameters can be known from the detector and others can be sampled jointly, so recovery remains conditional on the specified observation model. (low confidence)

Keehan, Anderson and Wiesemann calibrate Wasserstein ambiguity balls around weighted empirical distributions to balance sampling variability against bounded distribution drift. Their concentration theorem assumes bounded support, a bound on successive infinity-Wasserstein shifts, and independent observations. The resulting radius reflects both effective sample size and accumulated drift. The paper explicitly retains independence to focus on drift, so recency weighting here does not itself solve serial-dependence calibration. (low confidence)

Long proposes block multiplier bootstrap validation of a finite menu of Wasserstein-DRO CVaR portfolios. The preprint’s abstract describes a probability bound without an asymptotic remainder, while its conditional theorem includes a vanishing remainder. Treat this as an attributed CVaR validation proposal, not an established exact finite-sample Kelly guarantee. (low confidence)

In its diversification experiment, the Wasserstein-Kelly paper sets the ambiguity radius as a multiple of the average log return across assets and varies that proportion. This is an experimental radius parameterization, distinct from a procedure that inverts a concentration bound to certify a prescribed coverage level; its separate statistical theorem requires independent light-tailed draws. (low confidence)
Qingyun Sun’s public repository lists a Kelly optimization notebook. (low confidence)

Sun and Boyd define distributionally robust Kelly betting as maximizing the smallest expected log growth over a given set of probability distributions. Their finite-outcome tractability result supplies fixed-set context; it does not by itself select a statistical coverage level or a data-calibrated set size. (low confidence)

Mohajerin Esfahani and Kuhn give a concrete holdout procedure: solve the robust optimization problem for a finite grid of radii using training data, evaluate the resulting decisions by sample-average loss on validation data, and choose a radius minimizing that validation loss. Their k-fold variant averages the radii selected in separate holdout runs and refits on all samples. These procedures are presented within their IID sampling framework. (low confidence)

For the same dependent-data setting, Duchi, Glynn and Namkoong propose sectioning observations into consecutive blocks, computing robust optimal values within blocks, and studentizing the block results. Their proposition obtains pivotal Student-t asymptotics under the preceding theorem’s conditions. This is a justified block-based inference method with an asymptotic guarantee; it does not establish arbitrary block-bootstrap validity or finite-sample Kelly leverage calibration. (low confidence)

The Wasserstein-Kelly paper warns that a naive Wasserstein ambiguity ball for simple returns can admit negative portfolio gross returns outside the logarithm’s domain; even a nonnegative-support constraint can leave its worst-case expectation unbounded. The authors instead formulate ambiguity over log returns. For Kelly calibration, the modeled uncertainty variable and admissible support therefore need specification before a radius has a meaningful interpretation. (low confidence)

Timestamp aggregation and rounding require an observation-aware estimator: simultaneous recorded events do not establish simultaneous underlying arrivals. Filimonov and Sornette document packet bundling, and Shlomovich and colleagues explicitly model aggregated multivariate event data. (medium confidence)

Cheysson and Lang derive a Whittle spectral estimator for stationary linear Hawkes processes observed as fixed-width counts. Their count-spectrum derivation accounts for aliasing, and consistency and asymptotic normality require their reproduction-function moment and regularity conditions; these are stationary-model results. (low confidence)

Koyama’s coarse-grained Hawkes estimator accounts for intra-bin excitation using approximate conditional expectations under a uniform-within-bin assumption. The paper reports second-order matching and stable branching-ratio inference in its studied setting, but explicitly presents extension to nonstationary time series as future research. (low confidence)

For exact event times, time-rescaling by the fitted compensator gives unit-rate Poisson residuals under the correctly specified model. Assess transformed waiting-time distributions with quantile plots or Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests, and assess dependence separately, for example with the Ljung–Box test; the binned MC-EM study also compares transformed-waiting-time KS diagnostics. (high confidence)

Passing time-rescaling residual checks does not establish structural self-excitation: in Filimonov and Sornette’s regime-switching Poisson simulations, residual analysis fails to reject fitted apparently critical Hawkes models despite the absence of true event-to-event excitation. Such regime-switching Poisson data provide a concrete negative-control benchmark for estimator validation. (low confidence)

Jung and Lee distinguish three routes to additional identifying information: higher-order cumulants, restrictions on temporal model form, and an observed proxy for the common signal. Their third-order result gives generic local identification of normalized parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems, with finite-sample limitations under weak signals; it is not a general causal-identification guarantee. (low confidence)

Interval-censored event counts and undetected events are different observation problems. Rizoiu and colleagues model counts with unobserved within-interval times, while Deutsch and Ross model event loss or timing noise explicitly. A count-data estimator alone does not establish correction for undetected events. (medium confidence)

Finite calibration windows can underestimate the branching ratio by omitting triggering events before the window and offspring after its end, with stronger effects for longer memory. Filimonov and Sornette also identify outlier sensitivity, power-law-kernel regularization and multiple likelihood extrema as separate calibration hazards. (low confidence)

Jung and Lee establish generic local identification from integrated third-order cumulants for normalized structural parameters in two- and three-dimensional systems, but report weak conditioning and unstable estimates from empirical cumulants. They use restricted parametric spectral estimation in practice and explicitly do not report a calibrated over-identification test; theoretical identification is therefore distinct from reliable finite-sample recovery. (low confidence)
